metadata.title: What Happens To NVIDIA Stock If The Buyers It Funds Cannot Pay?

content.text:
NVIDIA (NVDA) now sits on both sides of its own boom. It has put nearly $50 billion into the frontier AI labs, has guaranteed a revenue floor at cloud sites hosting its chips, and will provide selective credit enhancement for nearly two gigawatts of compute at another lab. Management acknowledged on its August call that some would call this circular financing. So what if the buyers it funds cannot pay?
Is NVIDIA Already Funding Its Own Demand?
In part, and management has been open about the mechanics. At a NeoCloud site, NVIDIA provides a take-or-pay commitment on a slice of the capacity, which hands lenders a minimum revenue guarantee and collects a share of the rental revenue above that floor. It has also announced financing platforms with six infrastructure capital providers meant to raise over $500 billion of third-party capital.
None of that is small. OpenAI's existing and planned commitments come to about 12 gigawatts of NVIDIA compute, and management said in August that the labs leaning on its balance sheet should be about a quarter of the business in fiscal 2028. Management's line is that independent capital still underwrites each deal and that NVIDIA is not lending.
How Much Would NVIDIA Lose If Those Buyers Stopped Paying?
Less than the nearly $50 billion equity stake suggests. As a rough illustration across two different periods, that stake is a little under five months of the $127.0 billion of free cash flow NVIDIA generated over the trailing twelve months. Writing all of it down would hurt earnings at a company that still holds $24.1 billion more cash than debt.
The exposure that matters is the order book, not the write-down. Management says the compute it ships goes to investment-grade customers or buyers backed by one. So a lab in trouble stops ordering long before anything is written off, and collections are the earliest tell. They have already moved: days of sales outstanding stretched to 60 days in fiscal Q2 2027, on extended payment terms for large purchases by certain investment-grade customers to be shipped over multiple quarters.
Can NVIDIA Absorb It, And What Would Warn You First?
The cushions here are operational. Demand runs ahead of what NVIDIA can build: management guided fiscal 2028 revenue growth to about 70%, called it a supply-constrained outlook, and said customers' forecasts point to demand doubling. A buyer that steps back walks into a queue, and management says the platform it leaves behind can be redeployed to other customers.
NVIDIA reports fiscal Q3 2027 on November 17, against a revenue guide of $108 billion. Watch two things: collections and whether the non-hyperscale buyers, which management expects to be about half of the data-center business, keep adding capacity. Owning the shares through that means accepting real swings, because NVIDIA has fallen about 37% from peak to trough at its worst in the past three years. Our drawdown defenders ranking shows which stocks have held up best when markets turn.
